title: Trace instrumentation & token metrics pipeline — runtime/KV/batching deep dive with Nimbus Tech
summary: Deep technical session on integrating Redwood runtime traces and token-level metrics into Nimbus' observability stack. Covered OpenTelemetry spans and attributes for token index/kv cache hits/batching, recommended sampling strategies, export paths (OTLP -> Tempo/Grafana), on-prem agent considerations for VPC, and a proposed POC plan with a test harness and dashboards.
topics: OpenTelemetry span/attribute design for token-level metrics
next_steps: Ravi to share Redwood OTEL attribute spec and example OTLP config (link) (send by 2025-12-05)
Nimbus to provide representative request traces and sample payloads for POC (by 2025-12-08)
Schedule lab run: throughput test + token-level trace capture (target 2025-12-10)
Lena to send draft pilot commercial terms and estimated run cost
action_items: Ravi Patel: produce OTEL span/attribute doc + example config (2025-12-05)
Marta Ruiz: upload 6 hours of production-like request logs and sample prompt sets (2025-12-08)
Devon Lee: enable VPC egress rule for Redwood telemetry collector IPs in sandbox (2025-12-06)
Jin Park: provision Grafana workspace and Tempo instance for POC (2025-12-09)
transcript:
Header: 2025-12-03 15:30 PST | Duration: ~62 mins | Recorded via Fireflies
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jin Park (Redwood SRE); Marta Ruiz (Nimbus Platform Eng), Devon Lee (Nimbus SRE), Arjun Mehta (Nimbus SecOps), Priya Anand (Nimbus ML Eng)

00:00 Lena Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Lena from Redwood, this will be a technical deep dive — Ravi will lead on the runtime traces and how we emit token-level metrics. we'll aim to leave time for the POC plan at the end.
00:18 Marta Ruiz: thanks Lena, excited — we've got a mixed stack, cloud + some on-prem gateways, so really want to understand the VPC/on-prem story for telemetry.
00:26 Ravi Patel: cool, i'll start with the high level, then show a sample trace layout. quick note — transcription might mangle some names, sorry in advance.
00:39 Ravi Patel: First: we emit three things from the runtime: structured spans for request lifecycle (request.accept -> model.decode -> kv.lookup -> response.stream), token-level events as either spans or events depending on sampling, and aggregated metrics (per-second qps, avg token latency).
01:05 Devon Lee: when you say token-level events — are those full token text payloads or just token indices? security is a concern.
01:13 Ravi Patel: good question. We by default do not emit full token strings in production spans. we emit token metadata: token_index, model_variant, kv_cache_hit boolean, latency_ms for that token, and decode_op (sample/greedy/top-k). If customers opt-in for debugging we can include token text but it's opt-in and scrubbed.
01:36 Arjun Mehta: opt-in sounds okay, we need strong KMS controls and retention rules in that case. how does that work in the VPC private flow?
01:44 Lena Ortiz: in Private deployments we keep telemetry inside your VPC by running the Redwood collector sidecar or agent on-prem; export target is your Tempo/Grafana or your OTLP endpoint. keys and signing can be managed by your KMS — Redwood supports pulling secrets from your KMS/HSM.
02:02 Priya Anand: could you show a sample trace?
02:06 Ravi Patel: sure — i have a short example. (pauses) 02:12 — sample span tree:
02:12 Ravi Patel: span: request.inbound (attrs: request_id, user_id, route), child span: model.decode (attrs: model.name, seq_len, prompt_hash), child child: token.decode.0 (attrs: token_index=0, latency_ms=12, kv.hit=false), token.decode.1 (attrs: token_index=1, latency_ms=8, kv.hit=true), etc. we also attach batch_id when requests are coalesced.
03:01 Marta Ruiz: so token.decode.* — if you emit per-token spans that could explode cardinality in our tracing backend. how do you recommend sampling?
03:10 Ravi Patel: exactly — cardinality is the main tradeoff. our recommended pattern: full-span sampling for 0.1% of requests (trace-level), and token-level sampling inside those traces for 100% of tokens. For aggregated telemetry, we push token-aggregates as metrics: e.g., token_latency_histogram with labels {model_variant, kv_hit, batch_size}. That keeps Prometheus series limited.
03:41 Devon Lee: what does instrumentation look like for KV cache hits? is it emitted synchronously from the runtime or async as an event?
03:47 Ravi Patel: KV cache lookup is synchronous in the hot path. We emit a span 'kv.lookup' with attribute kv.hit=true/false and the cost estimate (cpu_nanos) for that lookup. For high-throughput paths we also emit a buffered metric update to reduce span pressure.
04:05 Jin Park: buffered metric update meaning you aggregate locally and push a counter every N seconds? what about crash semantics?
04:11 Ravi Patel: yes, local aggregation for frequencies; we flush on interval or on shutdown with a best-effort flush. On dedicated hardware we run a watchdog to attempt the flush; for air-gapped installs we recommend a persistent agent that can commit to disk and forward after connectivity restoration.
04:32 Priya Anand: are you supporting OpenTelemetry semantic conventions or custom keys for token-level attributes?
04:37 Ravi Patel: we follow OTEL for request and model spans but token attributes are Redwood extensions (prefixed redwood.token.*) — we can map to custom resource attributes in your collector. we'll share the mapping doc.
04:53 Marta Ruiz: how do you suggest we visualize this in Grafana? we run Grafana + Tempo + Prometheus.
04:59 Ravi Patel: ideal stack: OTLP -> Grafana Tempo for traces, Prometheus for rollup metrics, and a Loki pipeline for any decoded text dumps (if you enable them). We built example dashboards: "Token Latency by Model Variant", "KV Hit Ratio over Time", "Batch Size distribution vs Latency". We'll share Grafana JSONs.
05:26 Devon Lee: how do we connect OTLP from private deployment given we keep control plane separate?
05:31 Lena Ortiz: two options: 1) push-only: runtime collector inside the VPC pushes to your OTLP endpoint (no egress to Redwood). 2) pull model: Redwood-manager inside your VPC runs a collector that forwards to a managed sink under your control. For fully air-gapped, use local file-backed agent.
05:54 Arjun Mehta: if we want to keep telemetry off Redwood infrastructure entirely, do you support a binary we can run that writes to our Tempo only?
06:02 Ravi Patel: yes — the Redwood telemetry agent can be compiled into a static binary that speaks OTLP or writes to file. we'll provide the binary and its reproducible build checksum for security review.
06:13 Marta Ruiz: latency overhead — what's the expected tracer overhead per request if we enable token-level metadata?
06:19 Ravi Patel: when token-level metadata is emitted as events (not full spans) overhead is ~0.2%-1% per token depending on whether it's sync or buffered. If you emit token spans synchronously for all tokens, the overhead is higher and you'll see memory/rt impact unless sampling is used. We recommend aggregate metrics and selective token spans.
06:47 Priya Anand: about batching — when the runtime batches N requests, how do you correlate token events back to the originating request ids?
06:54 Ravi Patel: we attach per-request request_id and per-batch batch_id. Token events get token_index and origin_request_id. When reconstructing traces, Tempo groups spans by trace_id and we also surface a mapping table. There is a small perf cost for creating those mapping tuples but it's necessary for debugging MTL problems.
07:18 Devon Lee: quantization — does the runtime annotate spans with the quantization format used (e.g., 4-bit, nf4, int8) so we can correlate quality regressions to quantization config?
07:27 Ravi Patel: yes, model.decode span has attribute model.quantization=qn4 / int8 / fp16 and quantization_profile name if applicable. That helps correlate token-perplexity deltas.
07:37 Jin Park: can we add sampling rules by quantization_profile or model_variant? e.g., always sample if model_variant=stableA and quantization=int8?
07:45 Ravi Patel: absolutely — the runtime supports dynamic sampling rules: e.g., sample 100% for model_variant=stableA AND quantization=int8 for first 1000 requests per hour, otherwise 0.05%.
07:58 Marta Ruiz: what's the example OTLP config you'd recommend for our Tempo/Prometheus setup?
08:04 Ravi Patel: we provided a starter config in the repo: otel-collector-config.yaml. Key points: use batch exporter for Prometheus, set resource detectors to pick up k8s metadata, add a receiver for OTLP over gRPC, and add a processor that drops high-cardinality attributes from metric export but keeps them for traces.
08:29 Priya Anand: about high-cardinality: token_index is high-cardinality — how do you avoid series explosion in Prometheus when exposing token-level histograms?
08:36 Ravi Patel: do not label Prometheus metrics with token_index. Instead emit histograms aggregated by bucket ranges or by kv_hit/model_variant/batch_size. Token_index stays as a trace attribute only for sampled traces.
08:56 Devon Lee: we use Tempo + Loki. any recommended retention for token traces?
09:03 Ravi Patel: sampled token traces — 30 days is reasonable for debugging windows, but for security-sensitive tokens set retention shorter or configure obfuscation. Aggregated metrics can be kept longer.
09:18 Marta Ruiz: okay real-world question: our load peaks have 1.2M tokens/min in bursts. will your collector keep up or cause backpressure?
09:28 Ravi Patel: the collector is designed for high throughput; we recommend pushing aggregated metrics for those volumes. For traces, sample heavily. For on-prem, we can throttle telemetry export and prefer delta counters instead of per-token events. Also, we provide HV caching in the collector to reduce duplicate payloads.
09:52 Priya Anand: can we get a quick demo of a trace with batching turned on?
09:56 Ravi Patel: yes i'll walk through a recorded trace snippet. (screen share noise) 10:04 — Example: batch_id=bf-2025-12-03-11, batch_size=4; spans show model.decode with sub-spans token.decode.0..3. The trace shows token 1 had kv.hit=true and latency 7ms, token 2 was slower due to cache miss 45ms.
10:41 Devon Lee: that mismatch — can your dashboards flag token anomaly patterns automatically?
10:45 Ravi Patel: we have anomaly detection rule templates: if token_latency per model_variant exceeds baseline by X sigma, alert. We can feed that to your Alertmanager. We also generate regression alerts when downstream eval sets see quality drop tied to quantization_profile.
11:05 Marta Ruiz: we've got strict PII rules — how do you prevent tokens that look like PII from going to tracing?
11:12 Ravi Patel: we integrate a PII scrubber step before export. by default, token_text is not exported. For token_text debug mode we run a regex/smart classifier to mask emails/SSNs and we can auto-redact; also we can hash tokens with a salt held in your KMS so raw text isn't stored.
11:35 Arjun Mehta: consented. For the private deployment we need the agent to use our HSM to sign payloads. support that?
11:42 Lena Ortiz: yes, the agent can use your KMS/HSM to sign the telemetry payloads or to retrieve the encryption keys for the buffered store. we'll add that to the agent config example.
11:56 Priya Anand: costs — telemetry egress and storage — any rule of thumb?
12:01 Ravi Patel: big driver is trace sampling rate. Our rough numbers: sample 0.1% trace capture + full metrics = roughly 2-5% additional cost of runtime throughput; full token capture for 100% would be >100% additional. We'll send a spreadsheet with cost examples.
12:21 Marta Ruiz: let's talk POC. we want: 1) run a 24-hour production-like replay capturing token aggregates & sampled token traces; 2) validate KV cache hit tracing and dashboards; 3) confirm OTel pipeline to our Tempo; 4) performance impact <2%. Thoughts?
12:37 Ravi Patel: sounds good — proposal: spin up a sandbox deployment of Redwood Dedicated in your staging VPC, run a replay agent that sends real traffic; we attach Redwood collector configured for OTLP -> your Tempo. We'll run profiling and token-level sample capture.
12:54 Devon Lee: timeline?
12:57 Lena Ortiz: target lab window 2025-12-10 to 2025-12-12. we'll need the sample payloads and sandbox creds before then.
13:07 Marta Ruiz: who owns the sandbox networking?
13:10 Devon Lee: that's us; we'll open egress for collector IPs as per the doc.
13:18 Priya Anand: any caveats for quantized models on the dedicated runtime? we saw small jitter when switching quantization profiles during test.
13:25 Ravi Patel: jitter can occur when kernels switch; we recommend warmups and pinning kernel selection per rollout window. We'll attach kernel warmup scripts. Also in traces we mark kernel_switch spans so you can correlate.
13:41 Arjun Mehta: security review — we will need SBOM for the telemetry agent, reproducible binaries, and an access matrix for who can view raw traces.
13:50 Lena Ortiz: we'll provide SBOM and an ACL model. Redwoods' console allows role-based access to trace data and we can hook into your SAML SSO for RBAC.
13:59 Jin Park: quickly on observability cost control — have you tried delta-deduping for token aggregates?
14:04 Ravi Patel: yes, delta-deduping plus counter compaction reduces cardinality. We run compaction in the collector before export and apply label cardinality rules.
14:17 Marta Ruiz: great. final quick Qs: 1) sample config link? 2) dashboards? 3) estimated cost?
14:25 Lena Ortiz: we'll send three artifacts: 1) otel-collector-config.yaml and mapping guide, 2) Grafana dashboards JSON + Tempo query samples, 3) cost model spreadsheet.
14:33 Marta Ruiz: perfect, thanks.
14:36 Devon Lee: thanks all.
14:40 Lena Ortiz: recap — Ravi shares OTEL spec and example config by 12/5; Nimbus shares sample payloads and enables sandbox egress by 12/6-12/8; schedule lab 12/10. Action items listed in the meeting notes.
14:56 Meeting end.

Notes: Links referenced (shared in chat): https://redwood.example.com/telemetry/otel-attributes (Redwood OTEL attribute spec), https://redwood.example.com/telemetry/grafana-dashboards (Grafana JSON bundle), S3://nimbus-samples/payloads (Nimbus sample set)

Transcription quirks: some model/kernel names were auto-corrected (e.g., nf4 -> n f 4), speaker crossings at ~10:40.
